paper_title: Latent Feedback Is a Compute and Data Amplifier

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: When high-quality data runs out, a common practice is to train on it for several epochs, but each repeat is worth less than the last. Latent feedback, which feeds each token's top-layer state into the next token's input, is another way to spend that compute, yet it has not been tested against a vanilla Transformer that spends the same compute on more epochs. We run this test across a ladder of model sizes, unique data and epochs, tuning both models at every size and amount of unique data. Latent feedback makes every FLOP and every token count for more except when unique data is scarce relative to model size, a regime that today's models are far from. We find that latent feedback serves as an amplifier: with unique data fixed, it reaches a Transformer's loss with less compute; with epochs fixed, it reaches that loss with less unique data. Furthermore, both savings grow with unique data per parameter and with repetition, and downstream tasks agree. To go beyond our grid, we fit one scaling law to both models, in which latent feedback enters as a Transformer with more parameters; it predicts that both savings keep growing with unique data and repetition. Fitted on models from 60M to 271M parameters, the law predicts the losses at a held-out 778M size to within 0.3% and the gap between the two models to within 0.05%. At most, latent feedback saves 48% of the compute and 47% of the unique data. When data, not compute, is the limit, latent feedback is the better use of a FLOP for a model of a given size.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: High-quality text, not compute, now limits pretraining of large language models [1, 2]. Even web text, mostly not high quality, grows far more slowly than pretraining compute [3, 4]. So common practice is to train on the best sources for several epochs [510]. However, each repeat is worth less than the last, so additional epochs bring diminishing returns [7, 1012]. Latent feedback offers another use for that compute. latent feedback Transformer feeds each tokens top-layer state into the next tokens input. Prior work reports improved performance for extra training FLOPs [13, 14]. Yet these comparisons fix the training tokens, and none repeats data. With repeated data, the fair baseline is Transformer that spends the same FLOPs on more epochs. Whether latent feedbacks gain survives at scale, against vanilla Transformer given the same FLOPs and unique data, is still largely unknown. We therefore ask: When data runs out, can latent feedback make every FLOP and every token count for more? We answer it on ladder of models from 60M to 778M parameters, each trained on 12.5 to 400 unique tokens per non-embedding parameter (UTPP) for one to four epochs, that is up to 1,600 training tokens per parameter with repetitions (TPP). Both models are tuned at every size and amount of unique data, and the pools of unique tokens are nested and deduplicated. The answer is yes, once each parameter has enough unique data, and todays models have far more than enough. We measure the answer at fixed model size in two ways, and then fit law to extrapolate it. Compute. With unique data fixed, the Transformer must train more epochs to match latent feedback; it needs κ times the FLOPs (Figure 2 (a)). The saving grows with UTPP and with epochs: at two epochs, latent feedback costs 8% more at 12.5 UTPP, but saves 15% to 18% at 100 and 44% to 48% at 400. Above about 75 UTPP it saves compute at every budget we train, and at two epochs already above 33. Practice is far past this point: Chinchilla used 20 TPP [6], whereas today the median 1B10B dense model trains on 1,040, at least 260 UTPP even over four epochs [1517].1 Data. With epochs fixed, the Transformer needs µ times the unique data to match latent feedback with the same parameters and key-value (KV) cache (Figure 3 (a)). At one epoch on 50 UTPP, latent feedback saves 16% of the unique data at 271M and 20% at 778M; with three epochs on 100 UTPP, it saves 41% at 271M. fitted law for extrapolation. To go beyond our grid, we fit one scaling law to both models, with latent feedback entering as Transformer with times the parameters (Section 5.3). Fitted on 60M to 271M, it predicts the held-out 778M losses to within 0.3% and the gap between the models to within 0.05%. It then draws the boundary between the two regimes, FLOP spent on another epoch or on latent feedback, and predicts that both savings grow with unique data and repetition beyond the grid.

sections.content: Models. Both models, the Transformer and the one with latent feedback, share one backbone at 60M, 134M, 271M and 778M parameters. Its matrices train with NorMuon [34], normalized variant of Muon [35], and its embeddings and output head with AdamW [36]; see Table 10 in Appendix for details. Latent feedback uses = 0.15 throughout5, so its cost is about 1.20 to 1.27 across the four sizes. Data. We take the Dolma 3 sample [9] and process it ourselves: we deduplicate it and remove the documents that share paragraph with Paloma [37]. This keeps Paloma clean held-out benchmark for fair evaluation [38, 39]. We order its documents so that every prefix has the whole samples mixture of sources and topics with same ratios, and each runs pool is the first tokens of this order (Appendix I). Pools are thus nested and differ only in size, from = 12.5N to 400N. Tuning. We call one setting of model size N, unique data U, and budget cell. For each model, size and amount of unique data, we tune main run over the learning rate η and the timescale τ = 1/(ηλT) [40, 41], where λ is the weight-decay and the number of steps; other branch off the main run as decay runs and keep its hyperparameters. Each grid is centered on predicted start point from earlier runs and extended wherever the best point sits on its edge; cells value is the minimum of quadratic fitted to its points. Where unique data is small, we also shrink the batch to stay near its optimum [41]. Each main run uses warmup-stable-decay schedule [42] (Appendix G). Evaluation. We measure on held-out validation set of 47,274 documents (100M tokens), taken from the front of the same stratified order of the deduplicated Dolma 3 sample. It keeps the mixture ratio and excludes training documents. For downstream tasks, we score the Olmo 3 Base Easy suite [9], 109 tasks in 37 suites, as bits per byte (BPB) of the correct continuation on OLMES requests [43]. Each suite is weighted by the inverse of its seed variance, so noisy suites do not dominate (Appendix H). Decoding latent feedback token by token (Equation 1) is slow. We score it instead with 4 parallel passes of Equation 2, whose states h(4) nearly match the decoding states, so more passes leave the loss almost unchanged (Table 5 in Appendix C).

sections.title: 5 Experiment and result
sections.content: This section reads the grid of runs from Section 4 on validation loss in three steps, and then checks it on downstream tasks. First, with unique data fixed, we measure the compute that latent feedback saves (κ, Section 5.1). Second, with the epochs fixed, we measure the unique data that it saves (µ, Section 5.2). Third, we fit the law of Section 3 (Equation 3) jointly to both models, test it on the held-out 778M, and use it to explain the two savings and to predict them beyond the grid (Section 5.3). Finally, we check that the comparison is robust: repeats do not overfit, gaps are stable across seeds, and downstream tasks agree with the validation loss (Section 5.4).

sections.title: 5.2 Equal epochs: the data multiplier
sections.content: At equal size and epochs, latent feedback reaches Transformers loss with up to half the unique data (Figure 3 (a)). With size and epochs equal, both serve with the same parameters and KV cache; latent feedback pays only about 1.2 times the training FLOPs per token, and saves 1 1/µ of the unique data. At 271M and two epochs, for example, µ = 1.34 at = 50N, so latent feedback needs 25% less unique data than the vanilla Transformer (Figure 3 (a)). The saving grows with U/N and with epochs (Figure 3). At the smallest the two models need about the same data. The largest measured saving at 271M is 41% of the unique data, with = 100N and three epochs (µ = 1.69). At one epoch it also grows with size. Table 7 in Appendix lists every measured µ.

With the law checked at 778M, we use it to explain the two savings, to draw the boundary between the two regimes, and to predict the savings beyond the grid. First, the law explains the two savings: latent feedback trades epochs for capacity. Equation 7 has capacity term and data term, and latent feedback moves both. It lowers the capacity term, because it fits as Transformer with 1.14 times the parameters, factor that grows slowly with data per parameter and with size. However, it raises the data term, because its cost leaves it about 1.2 times fewer epochs, and repeated epochs still count: in the coupled fits, four epochs at 134M are worth 3.0 to 3.9 fresh ones. Latent feedback therefore wins where capacity limits the loss, and loses where data limits it. This is why both savings grow with unique data and with more epochs: each moves the Transformer toward its capacity floor, which latent feedback lowers. We want to point out the savings hold at fixed model size. Latent feedback spends times Transformers training FLOPs per token, as much as Transformer times larger, yet the law counts it as Transformer only times larger, and stays below (1.10 to 1.19 against 1.20 to 1.27). So when model size is free, simply spending the same FLOPs on Transformer times larger, with the same unique data, gives loss 0.006 to 0.012 lower in every fitted cell. That Transformer, however, costs times more per decoding step and holds larger KV cache, while latent feedback serves at the cost of the smaller model. Second, the law draws the boundary between the two regimes (the line κ = 1 in Figure 2).7 On one side of this line, FLOP is worth more as another Transformer epoch; on the other, it is worth more as latent feedback. The boundary moves toward less unique data as the budget grows: latent feedback wins from about 75 UTPP at = 1, 33 at = 2, 20 at = 3 and 12 at = 4. sections.title: 5.4 Robustness: repeats, seeds and downstream tasks
sections.content: Repeats up to four epochs do not overfit either model (Figure 6 in Appendix D). Even at the scarcest unique data, validation loss keeps falling through four epochs at every size. The gaps are stable across seeds: at 134M, gaps standard deviation is below 0.002 and none changes sign (Appendix D). Downstream tasks agree well with the validation loss  (Table 2)  . In Table 2, the Transformer has the lower BPB only at the smallest unique data (U 25N) and budgets of 2; latent feedback has it everywhere else, so the winner switches at almost the same place as in Figure 2. At = 4, latent feedback has the lower BPB in all 17 finished cells. On downstream tasks, latent feedback starts to win slightly earlier than on validation loss, and the two metrics pick the same winner in 59 of 71 paired cells (Table 6 in Appendix gives the validation losses).

sections.title: 6 Related work
sections.content: Spending compute on scarce data. With unique data scarce, prior work fits scaling law and, given unique data, compute, and fixed architecture, chooses the model size and number of epochs [12, 22, 27]. When taking architecture into account, sparsity in models delays the point where repeats saturate [45]; masked diffusion [46] overtakes autoregressive training once compute is abundant, across unique data and epochs. However, its gain needs excessive epochs: on 100M unique tokens its best loss comes at 500 epochs, against 50 for autoregressive training, whose hyperparameters follow prior recipe instead of being tuned per run. The looped model Parcae [47] spends extra FLOPs on loops at fixed parameter count, yet weighs them against fresh tokens rather than epochs. Latent feedback pays off within four epochs once each parameter has enough unique data, and we price it against epochs on fixed unique data, tuning both models at every size and amount of unique data. Recurrence in depth. Our law takes the same view: latent feedback enters it as Transformer with times the parameters. However, looped model still pays its extra compute again at every decoding step, even if it allows KV cache sharing [49]. Latent feedback recurs across tokens instead: it pays for its extra passes in training and in prefill, and generates each token like Transformer with one more cached vector. Feedback across tokens. Feedback memory [13] first fed deep states to later tokens but trained token by token; recent models feed back deeper layer [14, 5052] or frozen teachers state [53]. At equal compute or training time, some beat Transformer [14, 50] and others trail it [51, 53]. Yet none varies data repetition: even Wang et al. [14], who motivate feedback by scarce unique data, give the Transformer more tokens rather than more epochs. We compare against more epochs, across model size, unique data and repetition, and fit all three in one scaling law.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: We show that latent feedback makes every FLOP and every token count for more: once each parameter has enough unique data, it reaches given loss with less compute than more epochs, and with less unique data at equal epochs. Both savings grow with unique data and repetition, and one scaling law, fitted to latent feedback and the Transformer together, predicts them at held-out size. sections.content: Construction. Each raw file of the Dolma 3 sample holds one of 224 source-topic buckets. We keep the first copy of each exact duplicate, document with the same token sequence. We drop documents that share paragraph of 13+ words with Palomas validation or test sets [37]. These are 0.16% of the documents. We shuffle documents within each bucket. We then merge the buckets so that each advances along the stream at the rate of its token share. Every prefix is then stratified sample of the stream, so pools differ only in size. From 1B tokens on, prefixs bucket mixture lies within 0.003 of the whole streams in total variation.
